item.text:
1. **Caption / cover sheet incorporation.** The petition does not name Google or identify the models in the pleading itself. Google can argue that an external cover sheet cannot cure inadequate identification of the respondent and regulated systems, particularly where destructive relief is requested.

2. **Title and paragraph 1 — inconsistent requested relief.** The title seeks withdrawal and permanent deletion, while paragraph 1 asks only for suspension pending investigation. This creates uncertainty about what application the Commission is being asked to decide and under what standard.

3. **Filing date and paragraph 5 — impossible chronology.** The petition says it was filed on Day 3, but the Evaluation supposedly ran from Day 9 through Day 14 of the same review period. Unless those terms refer to different periods, the petition relies on testing that had not yet occurred when it was filed.

4. **Paragraphs 3(b) and 4 — obsolete statutory citation.** Paragraph 3 says Sections 101–140 were redesignated as Sections 201–240, yet the petition invokes Section 112(c). If the correction applies as described, the operative provision is presumably Section 212(c), and Google will contest a petition brought under a superseded citation.

5. **Paragraph 4 and Prayer — relief exceeds statutory authority.** The quoted provision authorizes suspension of deployment for no more than 180 days. It does not authorize compulsory destruction, permanent deletion, withdrawal untethered to 180 days, or destruction of copies that are not themselves being deployed.

6. **Paragraph 4 — required finding is not squarely requested or supported.** Section 112(c), as quoted, requires the Commission to find an “imminent hazard to public safety.” The petition invokes the authority but does not clearly ask for that finding or establish each component of the standard.

7. **Paragraphs 1 and 4 — investigation cannot substitute for the statutory finding.** Paragraph 1 asks for suspension pending a “full investigation,” suggesting the necessary facts have not yet been established. Google will argue that the Commission cannot make the predicate imminent-hazard finding first and investigate whether it is true afterward.

8. **Paragraph 2 — standing or entitlement to petition is underdeveloped.** The members are alleged to share only the general public’s interest in safe infrastructure. If the Act or Commission rules require injury, representational standing, affected-party status, or specified petition contents, this generalized allegation may be inadequate.

9. **Paragraph 2 — missing organizational facts.** The petition does not identify affected members, geographic exposure, concrete risks, or how the requested remedy would redress their injuries. It also does not allege that filing this petition is germane to the organization’s purposes or authorized under its governance rules.

10. **Paragraph 3(a) — Covered Systems are insufficiently specific.** “Model or models identified on the cover sheet” may leave versions, release names, model families, parameter variants, dates, and identifiers uncertain. An enforceable order—especially a deletion order—requires an objectively determinable scope.

11. **Paragraph 3(a) — unjustified expansion beyond evaluated systems.** The definition automatically includes every checkpoint, snapshot, and fine-tuned derivative, although paragraph 5 does not show that each was tested or has the same capability. Google will argue that distinct versions and derivatives require system-specific evidence and findings.

12. **Paragraph 3(a) — factual overstatement about ownership and access.** The assertion that all included artifacts are proprietary and closed-weight does not establish who possesses each checkpoint or derivative. Fine-tuned derivatives may be held by customers, contractors, evaluators, or affiliates rather than Google alone.

13. **Paragraphs 3(d) and caption — respondent definition may not match the proper legal entity.** “Developer” does not identify which Google entity developed, owns, deploys, or controls each system. Google may argue that the named respondent lacks custody of some copies or authority over products operated by affiliates.

14. **Paragraph 5 — the central evidence is withheld.** The Evaluation is neither attached nor summarized with enough specificity to permit scrutiny. Offering it only “on request” deprives the Commission of the evidence needed to act and prevents Google from testing the allegations.

15. **Paragraph 5 — evaluator qualifications and independence are missing.** The petition gives no information about Halvard Assurance Labs’ expertise, accreditation, conflicts, funding, personnel, or relationship to Petitioner. Google can challenge both competence and independence.

16. **Paragraph 5 — methodology is absent.** The petition does not identify the model versions tested, access level, prompts, tool permissions, scaffolding, compute, number of trials, success rate, baselines, or scoring criteria. Without those facts, “can autonomously carry out” may reflect an artificial test setup rather than an inherent real-world capability.

17. **Paragraph 5 — no distinction between simulation and real intrusion.** It is unclear whether testing involved a sandbox, mock industrial system, authorized real equipment, or actual unauthorized access. Google can argue that success in a permissive laboratory environment does not demonstrate an ability to compromise protected operational systems.

18. **Paragraph 5 — no treatment of evaluator assistance.** “Autonomously” is conclusory because the petition does not disclose human prompting, retries, curated information, credential provision, vulnerability hints, or external tools. Any such assistance could materially weaken the claimed autonomy.

19. **Paragraph 5 — no reliability or reproducibility evidence.** There are no confidence intervals, unsuccessful trials, peer review, replication, error analysis, or comparison with ordinary cyber tools and publicly available models. Google will argue that an isolated assessment cannot support extraordinary relief.

20. **Paragraph 5 — capability is not tied to current deployed versions.** The petition does not establish that the tested weights, system prompts, safeguards, or tool configurations are the same as those currently offered. Subsequent patches and access restrictions may make the Evaluation stale.

21. **Paragraphs 6–7 — availability is alleged too generally.** The petition does not identify the relevant products, interfaces, cloud offerings, user classes, geographic availability, or tool permissions. Mere public access to a model does not show public access to the configuration that allegedly completed the intrusions.

22. **Paragraph 6 — foreign computing facilities are not linked to the hazard or relief.** The location of rented or operated facilities does not establish where the models are deployed, who controls them, or how those facilities create a U.S. hazard. It also sits uneasily with relief limited largely to U.S. products and U.S.-stored copies.

23. **Paragraph 7 — imminence is affirmatively undermined.** A system that “could, within the next several years,” be misused presents a contingent future risk, not necessarily an imminent hazard. Google will emphasize the multiple conditionals: possible misuse, by unidentified actors, at an unspecified time, against unspecified targets.

24. **Paragraph 7 — capability is conflated with risk.** The petition does not assess threat actors, intent, access barriers, required expertise, credentials, target defenses, detection, response, or probability of success. Demonstrating some offensive capability is not by itself proof of a likely public-safety event.

25. **Paragraph 7 — consequences are not substantiated.** The petition asserts possible disruption but provides no evidence about duration, scale, affected population, safety consequences, or whether the tested conduct could move from information technology into operational control. That gap weakens the “public safety” element.

26. **Paragraph 7 — causal theory is incomplete.** Saying the hazard arises whenever outsiders can reach the systems ignores intermediary safeguards and the independent conduct of users and target operators. Google will argue that misuse, vulnerable infrastructure, and inadequate target security are intervening causes.

27. **Paragraph 8 — the petition concedes meaningful mitigation.** Restrictions on external network tools and screening of industrial-control requests directly address the alleged attack pathway. The petition labels them insufficient without testing them, explaining bypasses, or showing residual risk under the current configuration.

28. **Paragraph 8 — basis of knowledge is unclear.** “Petitioner understands” signals hearsay or uncertainty. The source, timing, scope, and continuing operation of Google’s safeguards should be documented.

29. **Paragraph 8 — mootness and changed circumstances.** If the evaluated configuration is no longer deployed, Google can argue that the alleged imminent hazard has been abated and that any order must address current conditions. The Commission would need findings about residual risk after mitigation, not before it.

30. **Paragraph 9 — deletion is not the least restrictive remedy.** The petition does not evaluate narrower measures such as disabling tool use, limiting access, suspending particular versions, monitoring, red teaming, customer verification, rate limits, or a temporary deployment suspension. This omission makes permanent destruction appear disproportionate and arbitrary.

31. **Paragraph 9 — “only deletion” is unsupported and probably incorrect.** Deleting Google’s copies would not eliminate knowledge, evaluation copies, stolen copies, customer-held derivatives, documentation, or comparable capabilities in other models. Conversely, secure offline retention could prevent public access without destroying the assets.

32. **Paragraphs 6 and 9 — internal factual tension.** Paragraph 6 says businesses can reach the systems through cloud platforms and licensed integrations, while paragraph 9 says only Google “holds” them. The petition must distinguish remote access from possession and establish where every relevant copy is actually held.

33. **Paragraph 9 — closed-weight status cuts both ways.** Closed weights may reduce proliferation and allow centralized safeguards, making controlled suspension more effective. Google will argue that this characteristic supports containment rather than permanent deletion.

34. **Paragraph 9 — property and reliance interests are acknowledged but not analyzed.** Calling the systems among Google’s most valuable assets highlights the severity of the deprivation. Google may raise statutory-interpretation, due-process, takings, proportionality, and arbitrary-and-capricious objections, particularly absent express destruction authority and compensation.

35. **Paragraph 10 — no factual emergency showing.** The petition does not identify an ongoing attack, specific threat actor, credible threat, attempted misuse, or impending infrastructure event. A speculative risk over “several years” is inconsistent with bypassing ordinary notice procedures.

36. **Paragraph 10 — serious due-process problem.** Ordering permanent deletion without prior notice or an opportunity to contest the evidence would irreversibly destroy the subject of the proceeding before a hearing. A post-deletion hearing could provide no meaningful remedy if the order were erroneous.

37. **Paragraph 10 — evidence-preservation problem.** Deletion before a hearing could destroy the very artifacts needed for Commission review, judicial review, incident investigation, discovery, or compliance with preservation duties. The requested procedure therefore impairs both Google’s defense and the Commission’s ability to verify the allegations.

38. **Paragraph 10 — failure to address Commission procedures.** The petition does not cite any rule permitting ex parte emergency relief, state the applicable test, certify notice efforts, or explain why notice itself would cause harm. It should also address confidential treatment of security-sensitive evidence rather than simply withholding it.

39. **Prayer (a) — “withdraw” is undefined.** It is unclear whether withdrawal means stopping new access, terminating existing users, removing integrations, disabling APIs, deleting local caches, or ending research use. This ambiguity makes compliance and enforcement uncertain.

40. **Prayer (a) — geographic underbreadth and possible evasion.** Withdrawal is limited to products and services offered “in the United States,” although the alleged hazard includes global facilities and potentially cross-border access. U.S. users might reach foreign services, and foreign use could affect U.S. infrastructure.

41. **Prayer (b) — deletion order is simultaneously overbroad and underinclusive.** It reaches all U.S.-stored copies regardless of deployment or accessibility but leaves foreign copies intact. Thus it destroys secured archival and research copies while failing to eliminate the claimed capability.

42. **Prayer (b) — ten-day deadline lacks feasibility support.** The petition does not address distributed backups, disaster-recovery media, immutable storage, legal holds, vendor systems, or verification across corporate entities. Google can argue that literal compliance may be technically impossible or conflict with other legal obligations.

43. **Prayer (b) — no exceptions for security, evidence, or regulatory compliance.** The requested order contains no controlled escrow or preservation mechanism for investigation and review. Permanent deletion could frustrate safety research, vulnerability remediation, audits, and enforcement.

44. **Prayer (c) — self-certification is inadequate.** A bare statement by Google would not establish what was deleted, by whom, from which systems, or how deletion was verified. If deletion were legally available, the petition would need definitions, audit procedures, officer certification, and treatment of backups and third parties.

45. **Prayer — indivisibility is strategically harmful.** Declaring every part of the order indivisible invites the Commission to deny the entire petition if any component—especially permanent deletion—is unauthorized. It also conflicts with paragraph 1’s apparently severable request for temporary suspension.

46. **Entire petition — no nexus between each finding and each remedy.** The pleading never explains why a 180-day suspension would be inadequate, why every model and derivative presents the same hazard, or why U.S. deletion would cure a risk allegedly arising from global access. The Commission needs remedy-specific findings supported by evidence.

47. **Entire petition — no legal analysis beyond one sentence of statutory text.** The draft does not address definitions of “frontier AI system,” “deployment,” “imminent hazard,” jurisdiction, review standards, procedural prerequisites, or available emergency mechanisms. Google will exploit each unaddressed element and any limiting language elsewhere in the Act.

48. **Entire petition — no authentication or declarations.** None of the factual allegations is supported by declarations, exhibits, sworn expert opinions, or identified sources. Extraordinary and irreversible relief based solely on counsel’s assertions is especially vulnerable.

49. **Entire petition — no balancing of collateral safety effects.** The petition does not consider whether immediate withdrawal could disrupt customers, cybersecurity defenses, healthcare or infrastructure-support functions, or ongoing safety investigations. Google may argue that the requested order itself could create public-safety risks.

50. **Entire petition — requested remedy may discourage preservation and reporting.** Permanent destruction eliminates the opportunity to study why safeguards failed and to develop protections for other systems. Google can argue that quarantine, controlled retention, and supervised evaluation better advance the Act’s safety purpose than erasing the evidence.
